utterances.text: Let's look at the first sentence. I think there is a typo here, but I suppose it says: "A big show was put on for Albright." We should look at the manuscript to check this. Can you read the first two items.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: "A big show was put on for Albright. She expected they would find 1.200 Muslim bodies at Pilica, but they found some five bodies."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: "We met Koljevic, Biljana and concluded it was best for commission to be formed on the basis of equal parity to rely [sic] investigate all deaths and killings around Srebrenica during the war."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at this item below, "If they expand the campaign ..." [In English] "If they expand." [Interpretation] Yes. You can count the -- there are four items before that.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: "If they expand the campaign, then they would form a joint commission (one for civilian security, one from army security, and two from UN) to investigate the killings of every individual." You want me to read the next sentences also?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: "Accusation of rape - Karadzic says that some lawyer in the USA is defending him well. "Crimes of such type have to address personally. "Defence costs of General Djukic to be paid. "All funeral costs to be paid --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you. Now, let's just look carefully -- I'll explain why I'm putting forward these examples. It concerns the admissibility and value of these documents. Do you agree that when I say, "If they expand the campaign," and I meant the propaganda campaign, then a joint commission would be formed, and the translation says, "they would form." [In English] "Then they would form a joint commission." [Interpretation] The translation sounds as if someone else was to form a joint commission, whereas Mladic writes that we were going to set up a joint commission. It's not quite grammatical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is not the moment to deal with the correctness of the translation of this notebook. You have ample opportunity to deal with or challenge the correctness of the translation. This witness has nothing to do with the translation of this notebook.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 1D2267. Let's bear in mind that this was 22nd March 1996. 1D267.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 2267.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2267. That is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I read it myself, because we don't seem to have a translation yet, although the OTP has a copy of this document. It's addressed to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, to the MUP of Republika Srpska, to the Defence Ministry, the Ministry of Justice and Administration, the Supreme Court, the Supreme Military Court, the republic public prosecutor, and the prosecutor of the Army of Republika Srpska. Can you confirm that this is dated 1st April, 1996?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe P00164 will be the translation, which would help the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. Can we see the translation as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that this document is dated 1st April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Can you read the document quickly, tell us what it is about, and if there is any connection between this and Mladic's entry in his notebook dated 22nd March 1996. That's sometime before this document. You don't have to read it all. Just tell us briefly what it is about.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: This is about victims of Srebrenica events. It's about possible investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I read myself. Is it correct that an order is given here to conduct a detailed review of the sites where there are victims of armed conflicts and to identify these victims? It's not about whether an investigation will be conducted or not. An investigation must be done. But this is an order to identify the victims, the cause of death, and certainly to establish whether they are civilian or military victims. Furthermore, to investigate whether there was any intentional murder of civilians or wounded people or prisoners of war, or whether any other crime was committed in violation of The Hague or the Geneva Conventions, the perpetrators of any such crime to be identified so that legal proceedings may be started without delay, and this order is to be implemented immediately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic? What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Do you agree, Mr. Blaszczyk, that with these diaries we need to have documents like this to understand the essence?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I don't think so. Diary is diary. If we are talking right now about authenticity of the diary, I don't think that we need any additional documents, this type of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the point of Mladic's documents is to jog his memory? It wasn't supposed to be a document to be used for any other purposes? What was the purpose of having written these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the purpose of keeping the diary is nothing to do with this witness. That's one thing. And I think I'm emphasising this point for third or fourth time. This is not the moment to deal with the weight or probative value of Mladic's notebook. This witness has been brought to testify to the chain of custody and the authenticity of them. Can I take it from your line of questions that you are not challenging the authorship by Mladic of this notebook, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. We are not disputing that these are Mladic's diaries. However, since the learned Mr. Nicholls was also trying to prove the authenticity by way of documents, the Defence wishes to say that the diary is not a document per se because it is not linguistically complete. Therefore, we have to be careful in terms of the admissibility and the usability of these documents. I am going to ask later on -- actually, I'm going to raise the subject of how these documents should be admitted. These documents were written as reminders for Mladic, probably for memoirs, or they're just notes. It's not a diary in the true sense of the word. So let us bear in that in mind. If that's the way it is, then I could complete this cross-examination. I could tender these documents. This order, if it is acceptable, then I would like to tender that. And then I'm going to ask Mr. Robinson to present our view of the admissibility and usability of these documents, these diaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. You'll have about an hour, less than an hour, to complete your cross-examination. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That has already been admitted as Exhibit P164.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If this line of questioning does not serve the purpose of corroborating this diary, then I'm done. As far as admissibility is concerned, I will give the floor to Mr. Robinson to say how we believe these documents should be taken, these diaries should be taken. I mean, I would be very worried, we would be very worried, if they were to be admitted in their entirety without additional corroborating documents and also establishing the true sense of everything that is stated, because these documents were just written for the purpose of reminding Mladic later on of something that had happened. So it's an aide-memoire, a reminder. It's not a diary in the true sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. You will have ample opportunity to -- to deal with the meaning or -- the meaning of these notebook entries or as to how to interpret them, and you'll have -- also have ample opportunity to make submission on that. I take it you concluded your cross-examination of Mr. Blaszczyk, and I wonder whether you have any re-exam --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, except that we should ask Mr. Robinson to present our position on the conditions under which this is acceptable and admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come back to that after concluding the evidence of Mr. Blaszczyk. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Blaszczyk. Thank you for your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You stated that after the testimony of the witness and the cross-examination of Dr. Karadzic, you will give us a clear answer to the authenticity or admissibility. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't contest the authenticity of the notebooks. So that's the first point. The second point is having reviewed the notebooks in their entirety during the recess, we believe that they're very helpful to the Defence and that there's many entries in these notebooks that can be very useful and corroborate what Dr. Karadzic has been saying all along. So we see that it's in our interest as well as the interest of the Prosecutor that entries from the diaries be used during this trial and be available to the Chamber. However, we doesn't think that it's fair for the notebooks to be admitted in their entirety as some kind of collection, because we believe that what is -- we don't have the ability to question General Mladic about what he meant or what -- we don't have the ability to confront him with these entries. So we think that what the practice ought to be is that individual entries be considered for admission as presented by consistent with testimony or other documents, similar to the 15 entries that Mr. Nicholls has on his chart and similar to the few documents and entries that Dr. Karadzic was giving as example in his cross-examination. So it would be our position that we should admit on an entry-by-entry basis documents or entries from the diary that are corroborated by witness testimony or other documents, and we feel that that would be the correct way in which these Mladic notebooks ought to be treated. And I would before sitting down also like to express our appreciation to the Chamber for having the next two weeks to look at the tapes, because I think we may come to a similar conclusion once we've had the opportunity to actually understand what's in those tapes. And having had the opportunity to finally see what was in the notebooks, we feel that they're on balance more useful to the Defence than we had expected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At the beginning today, Mr. Robinson said that he was putting the Prosecution to its proof before they took a position and would see whether we could prove or not that these notebooks were authored by General Mladic. We've done that, and they have now taken the position that there is no question but that these notebooks were authored by General Mladic. Along with the testimony of Mr. Blaszczyk, we went into the location of the notebooks, that they were seized from General Mladic's wife's home in Belgrade, and the chain of custody. I think we have met our burden it at this stage for admissibility of these notebooks. We have proven that there is beyond sufficient indicia of reliability for these to be admitted. I would move to admit all of the notebooks in their entirety. All of the -- the Chamber has found, in respect of the ones added to the 65 ter list from the second seizure, those notebooks, that they're prima facie relevant to these proceedings. We've seen today through the course of the proceedings how different documents and dates are corroborated by independent documentation, independent of the notebooks, and witnesses, indeed Mr. Karadzic was speaking about meetings he was present at and what he really meant and what should have been written down. So these documents are probative and will be helpful, and I think it the most utility, as with the Assembly sessions, although, of course, this a smaller set, is to have them in their entirety. All of the concerns, all of the concerns raised by Mr. Robinson go to the weight, which is something -- the weight of this evidence to be accorded in the final judgement, if any, is something, like any other piece of evidence, the Trial Chamber will judge after hearing all of the evidence in the case, all of the witnesses, comparing it to different material and then assign the correct weight. So all of the concerns raised that this was written by somebody we can't cross-examine, we don't know exactly what was in his mind, that can all be pointed out in the final brief and, indeed, as we go along where relevant and can be considered by the Trial Chamber in its deliberation. But as with the Assembly sessions, the Defence here have -- although they haven't agreed to them coming in in their entirety, have agreed that these are probative, that portions will be useful to them, and that these are authentic. So my submission would be to enter them in their entirety and the fairness concerns raised are ones that would appear with many other types of documents and can be dealt with adequately by the Chamber when it comes to weighing all the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, Mr. President. First of all, the difference we see between this and the Assembly sessions is that those were recorded essentially in their entirety by people with the duty to make an accurate record of that, so we think that the confrontation concerns are different than receiving a shorthand diary. Secondly, if you look at an analogous situation, back in the New York headquarters of the UN there was a collection of memos from the UNPROFOR officers like General Morillon who attended meetings during the course of this conflict, and we wouldn't be suggesting that all this whole collection be admitted so that the Trial Chamber would have all of the recollections of the UN personnel who attended different meetings during the course of the conflict, and essentially that's what the Mladic diaries are. They're his impressions and his notes from various meetings that took place during the course of the conflict, and we think that it's more consistent with your practice and with the right of confrontation that there be some link between the evidence in the case and the entry before the Court has the ability to assess what usage should be made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that must be right, Mr. Robinson, but that's exactly what the Prosecution are advocating that the Court does, and that's what the Court will do. So it's -- it's not a question of admitting these documents wholesale as proving of truth of their contents. The truth or -- and thereafter the weight of any content of the diary will have to be assessed according to its context and according to other evidence by which it can be measured and accepted or indeed reject. So while I understand your concerns, I think you can be assured that the purpose to which these diaries are admitted are going to be no more damning or any less damning than any other document. It's simply a question of weight to be adduced in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for 15 minutes, after which we will give the ruling of the Chamber. --- Break taken at 1.11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the arguments made by the parties. It is of the view that as the authenticity of the notebook is not being challenged by the accused and that there should be no question as to the relevance of the notebooks, they can be admitted into evidence in their entirety. The concerns raised by Mr. Robinson go to matters of weight to be admitted by the Chamber to the evidence at the conclusion of the trial. The same must be said in relation to Mr. Robinson's proposal to consider the admission of individual entries in a piecemeal fashion. It is for the parties to present corroborating or contrary evidence as they see fit and for the Chamber to determine at the end of the case whether entries in the notebooks have been corroborated. For these reasons, the Chamber will admit the notebooks into evidence in their entirety. The numbers will be assigned by the Court Deputy and will be informed to the parties in due course. We are going to assign each number for each notebook. Am I correct, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be the best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are a further two matters I'd like to deal with before we adjourn. The first thing is concerned with the Status Conference I referred to. As we have already intimated, during the period of suspension of the hearing of evidence, the Chamber wishes to hold a Status Conference to discuss the progress of the trial to date. We believe that it would be helpful to have a discussion on this issue in light of our experience over the past months and in order to hear the parties' views on how the trial can be moved forward more expeditiously. I should note that the Chamber has performed its own calculations on the length of the remaining trial, making use of the data available in our monthly time reports. We have done this on the basis of a four-day-per-week sitting schedule, as well as a five-day-per-week sitting schedule in order to assess the impact upon the overall length of the trial. Without getting into a discussion right now about the merits of a four versus five-day sitting schedule, I would like to say that we are concerned about the results of our calculation and are interested in exploring ways to ensure that the trial is indeed a manageable one in terms of its length and the volume of evidence with the parties. Having said that, would I like to hear from the parties now solely on the issue of the timing of the Status Conference. So I wonder whether there are any preferences for a particular date in the next two weeks when we might schedule it. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. There are certain dates during which I will be unavailable and other dates which are inconvenient in preparation for those conflicting dates but possible. So certainly the -- I can either address the specific dates at the moment or pass the information on to the court officer, but at a minimum the 30th, 31st of August, 1st and 2nd of September present -- are impossible dates for me. The Friday of that week should present no problem at all, and next week is problematic, but if the Court cannot otherwise accommodate, and I understand it's a fairly demanding request in light of the fact that I'm only leaving one specific date open, I would make all efforts to be available during next week, but as indicated, the first four days of the following week are not possible for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To be clear, you said it would be okay for you to hold it on 3rd of September, Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I usually don't go anywhere. I'm around. So whenever you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll have that Status Conference at 10.00 on Friday, 3rd of September. For the next matter, I would like to go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In accordance with the Chamber's decision of the 18th of August, the hearing of evidence is suspended until Monday, 6th of September, and in the meantime we'll hold a Status Conference at 10.00 on Friday, 3rd of September. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of September, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 25
